extracted.intended_audience: researchers, university and journal press officers, medical/science journalists, and science-communication researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how press releases about health/biomedical/psychology research should disclose study funding and authors' conflicts of interest, and how to code/evaluate such disclosures in press releases and related news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention of study funding in press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the press release reports a funding source (binary: reported / not reported).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases in the study reported any funding source 29% (2011) and 52% (2015) of the time. Reporting funding in the press release is associated with increased reporting of funding in subsequent news (eg, 22% vs 7% in 2011). The authors recommend routinely highlighting funding in press releases to increase downstream reporting in news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify type/category of funding source
rubrics_metrics.description: When funding is reported, identify the source category: industry, government, charity, internal/other, or none mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study coded the first-mentioned source and then coded whether industry funding was listed anywhere; studies could belong to more than one category. Examples: industry (eg, GlaxoSmithKline), government (eg, NIH, MRC), charity (eg, Wellcome Trust), internal/other (eg, university-funded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit mention of industry funding when present
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the press release explicitly states industry funding for studies that had industry funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured as the proportion of press releases for industry-funded studies that mentioned industry funding (14% in 2011, 41% in 2015). For coding/analysis, a study was included in the industry-funded subset if any industry source was mentioned, regardless of list position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention of authors' conflicts of interest (COI) in press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the press release mentions any declared conflicts of interest by authors, or explicitly states that there are none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting of COI in press releases was extremely rare in the datasets (0–2% where a COI was declared in the journal article). The authors suggest press offices could routinely include COI statements to improve transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report 'no conflicts of interest' explicitly when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the press release explicitly reports that the authors declared no conflicts of interest in the journal article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting of no COI in press releases was also very rare (0–1%). The study coded press releases for explicit 'no COI' statements as distinct from omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair and complete representation of the study's funders and COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should fairly represent the entire set of funding sources and conflicts of interest associated with the study, rather than omitting or selectively reporting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note they simplified coding to presence/absence and did not capture whether press release reporting fairly represented the entire set of funders or COI; they recommend press releases aim to represent the full set to enable readers to interpret potential entanglements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard headers in press releases for funding and COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Include standard, prominent headers/fields in press releases that list funding sources and conflicts of interest (analogous to journal article headers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper suggests adding standard headers for funding and conflicts of interest in press releases to routinely operationalise disclosure and make such information visible to journalists and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make press releases openly available and link to publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure press releases are openly accessible and contain links to the associated peer-reviewed publication to facilitate scrutiny and remind authors to declare COI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open availability and clear linkage to publications could help peers and readers verify funders/COI and may encourage fuller disclosures by authors and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criterion: press release must be based on an accessible peer-reviewed article
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating or including press releases in systematic analyses, include only press releases about health-related topics that are based on a peer-reviewed published journal article that the researchers can access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the study's inclusion criterion (health-related topic broadly defined to include biomedical sciences, diet, lifestyle, psychology). For reproducible evaluation, ensure the underlying journal article is retrievable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary coding of press releases/news for funding and COI
rubrics_metrics.description: For content analysis, code press releases and news stories simply for whether they mention funding (yes/no) and whether they mention conflicts of interest (yes/no).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors used a simplified binary coding approach for press releases and news. They acknowledge this does not capture completeness or proportionality of reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding rule: first-mentioned funder recorded and industry presence flagged
rubrics_metrics.description: When coding funding sources in journal articles, record the first-mentioned funder and also flag any industry funder mentioned anywhere in the list (studies may belong to multiple categories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study's coding protocol always coded the first-mentioned source and then separately flagged industry funding if it appeared anywhere; this allows classification into multiple categories (eg, government + industry). For industry-specific analyses, include studies with any industry mention regardless of position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability and adjudication procedures for content coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure coding reliability by double-coding samples or entire sets and resolving discrepancies by consensus or arbitration; report observed agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study achieved high observed agreement (92–99% across items) with second coders coding 28% (2011) or all texts (2015) and resolving disagreements by discussion or third-party arbitration. They did not compute kappa when agreement was very high and randomly selected one answer for some disagreements in 2011.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: include funding and COI in press releases to preserve trust and enable sceptical appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose funding and conflicts of interest in press releases because disclosure increases trustworthiness and allows readers (and journalists) to evaluate potential industry entanglements that may merit scepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue that non-disclosure may undermine public and professional trust and that including such information in press releases could increase its reporting in news, given the observed association between press release content and news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid omission of funding/COI due to lack of media policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that omission in press releases/news may partly reflect absence of explicit media policies about reporting industry funding; institutions/journals should adopt policies encouraging disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes only 3% of largest US newspapers had explicit policies about reporting industry funding; institutional and journal press offices adopting routine disclosure policies could change reporting norms.
